abstract: |
  Online labor markets make workers' self-presentation visible and easy to copy, a condition we call copyability.
  We ask: *How do workers compose their profiles under copyability, and how can the resulting composition still distinguish them in the online labor market?*
  We address this question through computationally intensive theory construction using 353,099 Upwork profiles and 2.34 million qualifying sentences.
  Exact sharing, defined by equality of word-five-gram sets, occurs in 25.9% of profiles.
  Two models organize the analysis.
  A sentence-level model with worker fixed effects identifies selective profile composition: occupation-specific wording and numerical content are less likely to be shared, whereas assurances, encounter formulae, and sentences later in the profile are more likely to be shared.
  A worker-level model connects textual composition and circulation families to market position, measured by posted asking rates.
  Authored-specific composition has a positive association and shared-generic composition a negative association; family-linked differences remain after accounting for geographic proximity and worker covariates.
  The shared-generic association persists across completed-job groups rather than disappearing with verified reputation.
  Robustness checks and a supplementary qualitative analysis qualify these patterns without replacing them.
  We theorize copying as a practice of profile composition and develop a process model with three propositions.
  Under copyability, workers combine authored and copied wording selectively; composition and circulation are associated with market position; and verified records do not substitute for profile composition.
  Copyability need not eliminate information but can redistribute it across a profile's composition and circulation relationships.
  Asking-rate associations do not establish client valuation, causal effects, independent composition, or verified template origins.

# Introduction

A freelancer's public profile brings together two very different kinds of information.
Completed jobs, recorded hours, and client ratings summarize work carried out through the platform [@HongPavlou2017; @MorenoTerwiesch2014; @Yoganarasimhan2013].
The profile description explains who the worker is, what the worker can do, and why a client should engage them [@BlythJarrahiLutzEtAl2022; @Gandini2016].
The first kind of information is produced through transactions and recorded by the platform, so the worker has little direct control over it.
The second is written by the worker and can be revised at any time.
Both are visible to prospective clients, but the description is also available to other workers.
A sentence about reliability, expertise, or client satisfaction can become part of someone else's profile without transferring the experience it purports to describe.

Signaling theory makes this difference a puzzle.
A signal separates senders only if some find it harder to produce than others; when any sender can produce it at no cost, senders pool and receivers learn to discount it [@Spence1973; @ConnellyCertoIrelandReutzel2011; @BerghConnellyKetchenEtAl2014].
Profile text is such a signal, because any worker can copy another's description.
On this logic, copied text should tell clients nothing, and workers should gain nothing from copying it.
Yet copying happens: freelancers read one another's profiles, clients notice copy-pasted text [@GussekWiesche2024; @BlythJarrahiLutzEtAl2022], and in our data a quarter of profiles share at least one sentence word for word with another worker's.
And profile text still relates to market outcomes, even alongside verified records [@HolthausStock2018; @YueHong2025].
Work on rhetorical signals shows that inexpensive text can matter when it accompanies costly signals whose credibility clients attribute to the whole signal portfolio [@SteigenbergerWilhelm2018; @PlummerAllisonConnelly2016], but it treats each text as its sender's own.
Signaling theory lacks an account of how text that circulates among senders can still distinguish them.

We call the conjunction of public visibility and inexpensive textual reproduction *copyability*.
Copyability is a property of the platform's information environment, not an allegation about the intentions of a particular worker.
It makes others' self-presentation available as a resource, so that copying becomes one of the practices through which a profile is composed.
Our research question is:
*How do workers compose their profiles under copyability, and how can the resulting composition still distinguish them in the online labor market?*

We investigate this question through computationally intensive theory construction [@BerenteSeidelSafadi2019; @MirandaBerenteSeidelEtAl2022].
Using public Upwork profile records, we construct a corpus of {{< var sentences >}} qualifying sentences from {{< var workers >}} workers.
Sequence-preserving text-reuse detection identifies shared wording rather than merely common topics.
We then organize the analysis around two models.
*Model 1* examines composition within profiles: which sentences are shared and which have no detected exact match?
*Model 2* examines whether composition distinguishes workers in the market: how are a profile's composition and its membership in circulation families, groups of shared passages that tend to be adopted together, associated with its posted asking rate, our measure of market position, including where verified records are available?
Descriptive analyses of how shared wording spreads across workers, and of where near-identical sentences differ, help interpret both models.
A supplementary qualitative analysis of theoretically sampled profiles illustrates what the estimated patterns look like in actual descriptions.

The findings do not support a collapse of textual self-presentation into interchangeable cheap talk.
Exact sharing occurs in {{< var exact-prevalence >}} of profiles, yet most of these workers share only part of their description, typically {{< var shared-sentences-median >}} sentences, and write the rest themselves.
What they share is selective: occupation-specific and numerical claims are less likely to be shared, whereas assurances, invitations to get in touch, and sentences late in the profile are more likely to be.
Across workers, authored-specific composition is associated with higher asking rates and shared-generic composition with lower asking rates, and circulation families add information beyond geographic proximity and worker covariates.
Most importantly, the shared-generic association does not disappear among workers with substantial completed-job records.

We develop these patterns into a process model.
Copyability is its central condition, profile composition is its practice, and market position is its outcome.
Profile composition is the combination of two concurrent practices, authoring and copying.
Three propositions state the mechanisms that link the constructs: selective composition, composition and circulation associations with market position, and non-substitution between records and text.
The account distinguishes three dimensions of textual signals: *content*, or what a claim says; *profile composition*, or how authored and copied wording combine in a profile; and *circulation*, or how copied wording is distributed across workers.
The distinction does not imply that we can recover a sentence's original author or externally verified source.
It explains why reproducible content can coexist with informative composition and circulation.

This account makes three contributions.
First, it establishes copying as a practice of profile composition.
That copyability makes copying possible is close to self-evident, but its consequences have not been examined as part of how self-presentation is composed under signaling.
We show that workers neither compose afresh nor copy wholesale: they combine authoring and copying selectively.
Copyability thereby organizes self-presentation instead of only threatening the credibility of a signal.
Second, we derive more detailed propositions from the findings about how composition is associated with market position.
Authored-specific and shared-generic composition are associated with opposite positions, and circulation families carry information beyond broad geography, occupation, and recorded work.
Textual self-presentation is therefore both individually composed and relationally structured.
Third, we establish non-substitution as a boundary to a reputation-centered account.
Verified records do not make the measured textual associations disappear.
The resulting theory is not that clients reward originality or punish copying.
It is that the informational structure of a copyable profile cannot be reduced either to its words in isolation or to the verified record beside them.

# Conceptual Background

## Signals, Records, and Credentials in Online Labor Markets

Online labor markets connect geographically dispersed workers and clients through digitally represented information [@Horton2010; @LehdonvirtaEtAl2019].
For services that are difficult to evaluate before delivery, clients confront uncertainty about competence, reliability, and fit, and about whether a worker is available at all [@Horton2019].
Because applications are cheap, workers apply widely and many openings never lead to a contract [@KokkodisIpeirotis2023], so clients screen quickly on whatever is visible.
Research on online labor markets accordingly examines reputation, standardized information, and provider characteristics in hiring and market outcomes [@HongPavlou2017; @MorenoTerwiesch2014; @AgrawalLaceteraLyons2016].

Signaling theory explains how observable features can help distinguish senders with otherwise hidden attributes [@Spence1973; @ConnellyCertoIrelandReutzel2011].
Work on online labor markets separates assessment signals, whose production requires possessing the quality signaled, from conventional signals, whose link to quality rests on social convention and which any sender can produce [@HolthausStock2018].
The classical expectation is that cost makes signals credible, and platform evidence is consistent with it.
When a platform removed the fee for a certification test, the certification's hiring and price advantage narrowed and workers certified under the new policy were less likely to deliver high-quality work [@BaiGaoGoesEtAl2026].
Employers avoided workers who offered a guarantee deposit that high- and low-quality workers could produce equally well [@GaoLinLiuEtAl2026].
Yet costless communication is not necessarily uninformative [@FarrellGibbons1989].
A free capacity status became informative on one platform because workers' later behavior matched what they had declared [@Horton2019], and rhetorical signals can organize interpretation of a sender without certifying a costly investment [@SteigenbergerWilhelm2018].

By *verified records* we mean what the platform itself records from transactions: completed jobs, recorded hours, and client ratings.
They have a particularly direct relationship to activity on the platform.
A worker cannot acquire a substantial completed-job history without doing the work.
Recorded histories can reduce uncertainty.
Achievement records predict supplier quality, whereas skill credentials do so only under some conditions [@KathuriaEtAl2021].
They are nonetheless neither complete nor free of strategic behavior and evaluation problems [@Tadelis2016; @Rahman2021].
Ratings are inflated and blend heterogeneous skills into one score [@KokkodisIpeirotis2016; @Kokkodis2021], and clients and contractors shape them through relational practices even under double-blind feedback [@Rahman2018].
Their absence is also a practical obstacle: workers without an established record can struggle to obtain the very work through which such a record is built [@Pallais2014; @StantonThomas2016; @LiangHongGu2025].

Whether records substitute for other signals is an open question.
Group-level cues such as country image matter when a provider has no individual record, and their role fades as individual reputation accumulates [@KanatHongRaghu2018].
A monitoring tool that verified ongoing work reduced employers' preference for experienced workers [@LiangHongGu2025].
The weight placed on any one signal thus appears to depend on what else is verified.
*Substitution* would mean that text becomes less informative about market position as records accumulate; *non-substitution*, that textual differences persist among workers with similar records.
Records, however, are only part of a profile.
The rest is text that workers write themselves.

## Profile Text as a Signal

Descriptions differ from records because workers can select, order, and frame their claims.
Self-presentation is not simply the disclosure of attributes; it also organizes how an audience encounters them [@Goffman1959].
Freelancers describe services, translate experience into promises of usefulness, and present working styles alongside credentials, while clients read both what workers say about themselves and what the writing reveals about them [@BlythJarrahiLutzEtAl2022].
Potential clients assess freelancers largely through the profile [@GussekWiesche2023].
Self-presentation is especially important where professional recognition is no longer supplied by a stable organizational affiliation [@BarleyKunda2006; @AshfordCazaReid2018; @PetriglieriAshfordWrzesniewski2019].

A growing body of work finds that the content and style of this text relate to market outcomes beyond what records capture.
Coded self-promotion is associated with higher one-year earnings and ingratiation with lower earnings, while a verified rating is not associated with earnings in the same model [@HolthausStock2018].
Similarity between a profile and a job opening is positively associated with being hired, whereas the feedback score alone ranks applicants barely better than chance [@KokkodisPapadimitriouIpeirotis2015].
Applications that are longer, closer to the job description, and less prototypical of their category are hired more often [@TroncosoLuo2023].
A more analytical writing style in a profile is associated with lower subsequent earnings, and the association is conditioned by ratings, badges, education, and platform hours [@YueHong2025].

What counts as specific is a matter of fit rather than of quality.
Skills in online labor markets cluster into categories, and diverse skill sets are associated with higher wages than narrow ones [@Anderson2017].
Gig work unbundles occupations into individual skills, so specificity is expressed through what a worker is hired for rather than through a job title [@VanSlagerenHerrmann2024].
Specialized services give freelancers more autonomy over their rates, whereas generalized services face price competition [@PulignanoMuszynskiTapia2024].
Yet more cohesive skill sets are hired more often but earn lower hourly wages [@Kokkodis2023], incongruent skills help in low-skill and hurt in high-skill categories [@FuEtAl2021], and a formal writing style is penalized outside technical occupations [@YueHong2025].
Specificity is therefore not rewarded uniformly; its value depends on occupation, outcome, and audience.

These studies treat text as the property of a single worker.
Each measures what one profile says, how it reads, or how it relates to a job, and none asks whether the same wording appears in other workers' profiles.
That omission is harmless as long as text can be assumed to be composed afresh.
It matters once anyone can copy what others have written.

## Copyable Text: A Puzzle for Signaling

Classical signaling logic makes copyable profile text a puzzle.
A signal separates senders only if some find it harder to produce than others; if a signal is easy to copy, all senders will use it, which destroys its informational value [@BerghConnellyKetchenEtAl2014].
On platforms, cheap and widely available signals have indeed been diluted or discounted [@BaiGaoGoesEtAl2026; @GaoLinLiuEtAl2026].
Studies of text in these markets sometimes assume instead that detailed writing is costly to produce and therefore credible [@AlshalfanMahdikhani2026], without testing whether it is copied.

Profile text is easy to copy.
Digital artifacts such as profile descriptions are editable and reproducible, and their informational properties are shaped by the systems through which they are represented and accessed [@KallinikosAaltonenMarton2013].
Profiles are also public, so freelancers can read one another's descriptions and observe one another's career paths [@GussekWiesche2024].
Copying is also visible to clients, who report noticing copy-pasted proposals and stolen portfolio material and read them as laziness [@BlythJarrahiLutzEtAl2022].
Unlike a badge or a deposit, however, a copied sentence carries no label that distinguishes it from composed text.
Reused text is not peculiar to freelancing.
Copied passages appear in residency application essays [@SegalGelfandHurwitzEtAl2010], app stores contain copycat apps that imitate original ones [@WangLiSingh2018], crowdfunding updates repeat clichés [@BaoLeeZhang2025], and IPO prospectuses repeat standard content from earlier prospectuses in the same industry [@HanleyHoberg2010].
In these settings, too, reused text tends to carry standard rather than specific content.

Yet, as the studies reviewed above show, profile text relates to outcomes even alongside verified records.
Work on rhetorical signals explains why inexpensive text can matter: clients attribute the credibility of costly signals to the whole signal portfolio, including the rhetoric that accompanies them [@SteigenbergerWilhelm2018; @PlummerAllisonConnelly2016].
Like the studies of profile text, however, it treats each text as its sender's own.
Signaling theory therefore lacks an account of how text that circulates among senders can still distinguish them, and studies that measure each profile in isolation cannot provide one.

If wording circulates, it need not circulate evenly.
Online work connects distant participants, but place still matters.
Country image shapes provider outcomes when individual records are thin [@KanatHongRaghu2018], and geographic and social distance remain relevant to exchange [@GefenCarmel2008; @HongPavlou2017; @LehdonvirtaEtAl2019].
Workers also learn to navigate platforms informally, often outside formal organizations [@SutherlandJarrahiDunnNelson2020].
Place, occupation, and the period in which a description was created are therefore plausible dimensions along which wording could be shared.

This leaves the question that guides our study: *How do workers compose their profiles under copyability, and how can the resulting composition still distinguish them in the online labor market?*

# Research Method

## Computationally Intensive Theory Construction

We adopted a data-driven approach that iterates between computational patterns and theoretical interpretation [@BerenteSeidelSafadi2019; @MirandaBerenteSeidelEtAl2022; @Lindberg2020].
Interpretations changed over these iterations; for example, counting distinct adoptions instead of matching pairs showed that a few dominant passages did not represent most sharing, which redirected the analysis toward selective composition and structured circulation.
Text-reuse detection makes shared wording observable at a scale at which reading profiles alone cannot establish its distribution.
The technique comes from political science, where it traces how bill text moves between legislators and legislatures [@WilkersonEtAl2015; @LinderEtAl2020; @GavaJaquetSciarini2021].
Unlike topic models and other document-level text-as-data methods [@GrimmerStewart2013], which describe the themes that documents share, it identifies the specific passages that recur across documents.
We use it to show where in a profile reuse occurs and who shares it.
Statistical models then characterize relationships within and across profiles.
Interpretation relates these relationships to the concepts of the Conceptual Background: signaling, copyability, circulation, and substitution.
Consistent with computationally intensive theory construction, the models support theory development rather than a claim of independent confirmatory testing.

The analytic sequence in @fig-method has five phases.
We first construct the sentence corpus from the public profiles.
A separate text-reuse phase then detects cross-worker reuse, validates the similarity scores, and describes reuse for sentences, workers, recurring passages (scripts), and groups of passages adopted together (families); its output is the input to both models.
The main analysis estimates Model 1 and Model 2, together with the content, function, position, and variant-alignment descriptions and the verified-record, city, and circulation-family components that inform their interpretation.
The secondary analysis has two parts: a qualitative reading of theoretically sampled profiles and near-copy pairs, which draws its cases from the patterns the models identify, and robustness checks on alternative measurements, samples, and outcomes.
The final phase develops a theoretical model and propositions from these results.

![Analytic organization. Text-reuse detection precedes both models, which supply the principal evidence; content and variant descriptions and circulation components inform their interpretation. The qualitative analysis and the robustness checks follow the models and respond to their results. Arrows indicate analytic organization, not identified causal effects.](analysis/output/paper/figures/method.png){#fig-method}

The two models answer different questions at different units of analysis.
A worker-level comparison alone cannot distinguish selective composition inside a profile from differences in who participates in reuse, and a sentence-level comparison alone cannot show how the resulting composition relates to market position.
The two-model design connects these levels without treating them as a single causal sequence.

## Setting and Data Collection

Upwork provides a useful setting because workers present diverse knowledge services through public profiles that combine editable descriptions, asking rates, and platform-recorded work.
The input file contains {{< var raw-profiles >}} worker-profile records.
Data were collected on September 21, 2023, in a single run through public Upwork API endpoints.
A scraper assembled unique worker identifiers from Upwork's public category pages, which are organized by occupational category, subcategory, and occupation.
A profile-detail script then retrieved the public record for each listed identifier.

The collection aimed to retrieve every public profile, but its completeness cannot be verified against the platform's records, so we treat the data as a large cross-section of retrieved profiles rather than a census.
No claim that the collection covers every occupation or all active workers is required for the within-corpus analysis.

Besides the description, each record contains the posted hourly rate, completed jobs, recorded hours, rating, listed occupations, country, city, and agency affiliation.
Two timestamps record when the description was created and last updated; they do not date the account.
We measure *description age* from the description's creation to the latest update observed in the data, September 8, 2023 (Appendix A).

We took several safeguards.
The analysis uses only public profile text and metadata.
Workers are identified by neither platform identifiers nor names, and the paper reproduces no complete description or client name.
We quote only short passages that recur across workers, namely exact-shared sentences and, where we show personalization, near-copy variants.
Because each such passage appears, in identical or near-identical form, in more than one worker's profile, quoting it does not by itself identify any one worker.
We paraphrase unshared, personal, and client material.
Full profiles, identifiers, and case comparisons are internal research materials, not publication supplements.

## Corpus Construction and Reuse Detection

We first remove descriptions that share no common vocabulary with the rest of the corpus, a filter inherited from the original detection pipeline: a description must contain at least one non-stopword token without digits that occurs more than 100 times in the input file.
This retains {{< var filtered-profiles >}} profiles.
The filter favors English descriptions but is not a language classifier.
We normalize whitespace, segment descriptions with a sentence tokenizer, and retain units containing 8–50 whitespace-counted words.
The resulting reuse frame contains {{< var sentences >}} sentences in {{< var workers >}} profiles.
Counts of words for eligibility and tokens for content analysis use different tokenization rules, documented in Appendix B.

Each sentence is lowercased and represented by a set of word five-grams.
For sentence shingle sets $A$ and $B$, similarity is

$$
J(A,B)=\frac{|A\cap B|}{|A\cup B|}.
$$

This measure preserves local word sequence rather than only thematic vocabulary [@Broder1997; @WilkersonEtAl2015].
Comparing every pair of {{< var sentences >}} sentences is impractical, so we first generate candidate pairs and then compute their exact Jaccard scores.
Candidates come from MinHash signatures with 240 permutations [@Broder1997] and locality-sensitive hashing with 60 bands of four rows.
This configuration almost always detects pairs with $J\geq .5$ (see below) while keeping the number of candidates manageable.
Even so, rebuilding the derived data and fitting both models and the robustness checks takes about 1.5 hours on 16 cores (Appendix E).
Candidate generation produces {{< var scored-pairs >}} scored pairs; {{< var same-worker-pairs >}} same-worker pairs are excluded.

The main definition of *exact sharing* is $J=1$: equality of word-five-gram sets across workers.
It is not character-by-character identity.
Punctuation and case normalization, tokenization, and the use of sets can make surface forms differ while their measured sets are equal.
A *script* is a connected component of exact-sharing sentences held by at least two workers.
A sentence is operationally *authored* when it has no detected exact cross-worker match.
This category includes non-exact near-copies but cannot establish independent composition.

Candidate detection is similarity-dependent.
Under the LSH configuration, the probability of becoming a candidate is $1-(1-J^4)^{60}$: approximately {{< var lsh-low >}} at $J=.3$ and {{< var lsh-half >}} at $J=.5$, approaching one at higher similarities.
We consequently center inference on exact sharing, use $J\geq .7$ as a model sensitivity check, and use $.5\leq J<1$ for variant alignment.
Low-similarity candidates are not an exhaustive census of weaker reuse.
Nor do unobserved matches outside this corpus establish originality.

## Constructs and Measurements

Three dimensions of a textual signal frame the patterns surfaced by the analysis and organize the measurements and models below.
*Content* is what a sentence claims: its occupational detail, numerical claims, and rhetorical function.
*Profile composition* is how two practices, authoring and copying, combine across that content within a profile.
We observe authoring as sentences with no detected exact cross-worker match (authored) and copying as sentences with an exact cross-worker match (exact-shared).
*Circulation* is how copied wording is distributed across workers.
The dimensions can carry different information.
The same assurance can appear in many profiles, but its prevalence within a particular composition and its co-occurrence with other passages can identify a more particular presentation pattern.
Two constructs lie outside the text.
We operationalize *market position* as the posted asking rate and examine ratings and recorded hours as alternative outcomes in the robustness checks.
*Verified records* enter Model 2 as completed-job groups, whose interactions with composition test whether records substitute for text.
Copyability is a condition of the setting and is not measured.
@tbl-measures summarizes the dimensions, their constructs and measures, and the role each plays in the two models; control variables are listed with Model 2 below.

| Dimension | Construct | Role | Operationalization | Interpretation and boundary |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Content | Occupational specificity | Model 1 predictor; content split in Model 2 | Distinct informative word types; informative if used by at least 100 workers and occupational KL divergence is at least .5 bits | Occupational concentration, not uniquely personal truth |
| Content | Numerical content | Model 1 predictor | At least one numeric token under the content tokenizer | Can concern history, quantities, or service promises |
| Content | Rhetorical function | Model 1 predictor | Dictionary moves collapsed to claim-bearing, assurance, encounter formula, or other | Claim-bearing combines identity, credential, capability; estimation label: “individuating claim” |
| Profile composition | Authoring and copying (authored and exact-shared sentences) | Model 1 outcome; basis of the Model 2 shares | Exact-shared: cross-worker word-five-gram match at $J=1$ [@WilkersonEtAl2015; @LinderEtAl2020]. Authored: no detected exact match | Shared measured form, not verified copying intent or direction; authored includes non-exact near-copies |
| Profile composition | Sentence position | Model 1 predictor | Relative position among qualifying sentences: 0 for the first, 1 for the last | Index among qualifying units; does not necessarily equal literal position in the description text |
| Profile composition | Composition shares | Model 2 predictor | Authored-specific, shared-generic, shared-specific sentence shares; authored-generic omitted | Shares sum to one across the four categories |
| Circulation | Circulation family | Model 2 predictor (form 2c) | Co-adoption components of scripts; dominant family for each sharer | Circulation-based proxy, not an externally verified origin |
| Outside the text | Verified record | Model 2 moderator | Completed-job groups: 0, 1–9, 10–49, 50+ [cf. @Pallais2014; @KanatHongRaghu2018; @KathuriaEtAl2021] | Platform-recorded work, distinct from textual claims about experience |
| Outside the text | Market position | Model 2 outcome | Posted asking rate: log posted hourly rate, USD 3–500 [cf. @MorenoTerwiesch2014; @Kokkodis2023] | Asking price, not realized wage or observed client valuation |
| Condition | Copyability | Condition of the setting | Not measured: public visibility of profiles combined with inexpensive textual reproduction | Property of the platform's information environment, not of individual workers |

: Dimensions, constructs, and measurements {#tbl-measures}

**Content.**
We estimate a specificity lexicon on sentences with no detected sharing at $J\geq .5$, counting each worker once per word type.
For a word's users, we compare the distribution of first-listed occupations with the corresponding worker baseline using Kullback–Leibler divergence.
Types used by at least 100 workers and carrying at least .5 bits of divergence, excluding numeric types, are informative.
The lexicon contains {{< var lexicon >}} informative types.
A sentence is specific if it contains at least one informative type; the same indicator enters Model 1 and divides the Model 2 composition shares.
Estimating the lexicon on less-shared text reduces the possibility that a circulating template manufactures its own occupational specificity, but does not independently validate the construct.
A sentence has numerical content if it contains at least one numeric token (Appendix B).
We use occupational wording and numerical content as indicators of how narrowly a claim applies, not as measures of whether a sentence is true for one worker alone.
For rhetorical function, a transparent, ordered dictionary assigns moves before they are collapsed for Model 1.
Identity, credential, and capability moves form the reference group; character and process moves are assurances; encounter moves include invitations and courtesies.
Agency and unmatched moves fall in “other” in the model.
We use “claim-bearing” as readable shorthand for the reference grouping, not as a change to the estimation labels.
The ordered rules can privilege an assurance keyword over an occupational or testimonial function in a mixed sentence.
We retain this dictionary measurement and document supplementary disagreement diagnostics between the dictionary and the sentence codes from the qualitative analysis, without treating either as a benchmark.

**Profile composition.**
At the sentence level, profile composition is a sentence's exact-shared or authored status together with its relative position, which runs from 0 for a profile's first qualifying sentence to 1 for its last.
At the worker level, the four composition shares cross exact-shared or authored status with specific or generic content, so that authored-specific, authored-generic, shared-specific, and shared-generic shares sum to one.

**Circulation.**
To identify passages that recur together, scripts with at least five adopters are linked when at least three workers hold both and the overlap coefficient—co-adopters divided by the smaller script's adopter count—is at least .5.
Connected components form multi-script circulation families; unlinked scripts retain their own family identifiers.
A worker's dominant family covers the largest number of that worker's shared sentence instances, with ties favoring the family represented by a larger script.
This assignment summarizes circulation but does not represent all memberships of workers who combine several families.
Locality, cohort proximity, and price-peer comparisons describe the relational structure of reuse separately from the asking-rate model.
